newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to back campaign finance reform.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to back campaign finance reform.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, trying to defuse an uproar over fundraising by Democrats, planned to defend his efforts but renew a call for overhauling a system critics say invites influence peddling.

Starting his day on former Republican President Ronald Reagan's home turf of Santa Barbara, Clinton on Friday was set to make his first extensive public remarks on the attacks by political rivals Bob Dole and Ross Perot, who have been challenging the fundraising efforts by Democrats.

Clinton intends to chide Republicans for failing to enact federal campaign finance reform legislation while defending the decision by his campaign and the Democratic Party to aggressively build a political nest egg.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Clinton intended to argue that it was necessary for Democrats to fill campaign coffers "because of the nature of the law and the reality of the political challenge that we face in this election year."
"One thing he will suggest ... is that we need to reform those laws to minimise the kind of ... priority that has to be placed on fundraising," McCurry said.

With only days remaining before Tuesday's elections, the 1996 presidential campaign has become the most expensive in U.S. history -- with both the Clinton and Dole camps spending and raising money as never before. Both sides accuse the other of breaking election laws.
Clinton has been dealing with questions about a senior Democratic fundraiser's ties to the White House. The controversy has dominated the final days of the presidential race.

The Washington Post and New York Times report that John Huang, who was suspended from his Democratic Party fundraising duties two weeks ago amid reports that he unlawfully solicited foreign contributions, had made at least 78 visits to the White House since July 1, 1995.

Clinton has given unusual personal attention to fundraising efforts. Although he took care of all of his campaign's financial needs last year, Clinton has been readily available for events designed to raise money for the Democratic Party and its candidates.

Since 1976 at least 10 campaign finance reform measures have emerged in Washington, only to fade away before becoming law. The latest attempt was killed by the Senate this year, following opposition from Dole while he was Republican leader.

In the summer of 1995, Clinton and Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich shook hands during a joint appearance in New Hampshire and pledged to form a commission to reform campaign finance laws. Clinton appointed members to the panel a short time later, but Gingrich never did.

In 1974 Congress limited campaign contributions and spending and provided taxpayer funds for presidential elections. Two years later the Supreme Court found that such limits violated the First Amendment right to free speech. This year, the court issued another ruling that gave political parties even more freedom to spend money on congressional races.
Much of the current controversey centres on so-called "soft money" donations to the political parties, ostensibly to be used for party-building activities such as voter registration.

Even without "soft money," this year's presidential campaign is the richest to date, according to the spending limits set by the Federal Election Commission. Dole and Clinton can spend $138.7 million apiece from the first primary contest through Election Day.
